questions.q: List the two internal sources of recruitment mentioned in the NCERT textbook for Class 12 Business Studies.
questions.a: The two internal sources are transfers and promotions. A wrong answer (e.g., "advertisement and campus recruitment") reveals the student cannot distinguish between internal and external sources, indicating they have not memorised the basic classification from the textbook.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why internal recruitment is considered more economical than external recruitment.
questions.a: Internal recruitment is more economical because it avoids costs of advertising, agency fees, and extensive screening processes; candidates are already known to the organisation, reducing selection time and induction training expenses. A wrong answer that only says "it is cheaper" without mentioning specific cost components (advertising, agency fees, induction) shows superficial understanding — the student recalls the conclusion but not the reasoning.

questions.q: A company has a surplus of 20 employees in its accounting department and a shortage of 15 employees in its payroll department. Both departments require similar basic accounting skills. Which internal source of recruitment would be most suitable? Justify your choice in two sentences.
questions.a: Transfers would be most suitable because they allow horizontal movement of employees from a surplus department to a deficit department with similar skill requirements, utilising existing staff without changing their status or salary significantly. A wrong answer suggesting "promotions" reveals the student confuses horizontal movement (transfer) with vertical movement (promotion) and does not understand that promotions involve higher responsibility and pay, which is unnecessary here.

questions.q: Compare the impact of internal recruitment and external recruitment on the motivation of existing employees. Provide two distinct points for each source.
questions.a: Internal recruitment: (1) Motivates employees by offering career advancement through promotions, creating a chain of promotional opportunities at lower levels; (2) Builds loyalty and commitment as employees see a future within the organisation. External recruitment: (1) Can demotivate existing staff who feel their promotion chances are reduced, leading to frustration; (2) May stimulate healthy competition, forcing current employees to upskill to compete with outsiders. A wrong answer that only lists positive effects for one source and negative for the other shows inability to analyse both sides — a common board exam error where students take a one-sided view.

questions.q: "External recruitment always brings fresh talent but at a high cost." Critically evaluate this statement by providing two arguments supporting it and two arguments challenging it.
questions.a: Supporting arguments: (1) External sources like campus recruitment and advertisements attract a large pool of new candidates with updated skills and diverse perspectives, infusing "new blood"; (2) It avoids inbreeding and stagnation that can result from over-reliance on internal promotions. Challenging arguments: (1) External recruitment is not always high-cost — employee referrals and casual callers can be low-cost external sources; (2) Fresh talent does not guarantee better performance — external hires may lack organisational culture fit, require longer induction, and have higher turnover, increasing hidden costs. A wrong answer that simply agrees or disagrees without balanced arguments fails the "evaluate" command word, which requires weighing both sides — a pattern that loses marks in CBSE long-answer questions.

questions.q: Design a recruitment strategy for a new-age Indian fintech startup that needs to hire 10 software developers within 30 days. The startup has 15 existing employees, limited brand recognition, and a tight budget. Specify which sources (internal/external) you would use, in what order, and why.
questions.a: A good answer: (1) First, use internal source — employee referrals (existing staff recommend developers from their network) — low cost, high trust, fast. (2) Second, use external low-cost sources — web publishing on niche tech job portals (e.g., AngelList, LinkedIn) and campus recruitment from tier-2/3 engineering colleges — wider reach, moderate cost. (3) Avoid expensive sources like placement agencies or TV advertising. (4) If urgent gaps remain, consider direct recruitment via coding hackathons. A poor answer that suggests only one source (e.g., "just advertise on LinkedIn") or ignores budget/brand constraints shows inability to synthesise multiple concepts (cost, speed, quality, employer branding) into a coherent strategy — the essence of "create" level thinking.
